plan.contextChunk:
property: conditional on $x_2$, variable $x_3$ is independent of
variable $x_1$. The joint probability of all the variables shown here is
$p(x_1, x_2, x_3, y_1, y_2, y_3) =  \phi_{12}(x_1, x_2)  \phi_{23}(x_2, x_3)
\psi_{1}(y_1, x_1) \psi_{2}(y_2, x_2) \psi_{3}(y_3, x_3)$. Using
$p(a,b) = p(a \bigm | b) p(b)$, we can also write the probability of the
$x$ variables conditioned on the observations $y$,
$$p(x_1, x_2, x_3 \bigm | y_1, y_2, y_3) =  
\frac{1}{p(\mathbf{y})} \phi_{12}(x_1, x_2)  \phi_{23}(x_2, x_3) \psi_{1}(y_1, x_1) \psi_{2}(y_2, x_2) \psi_{3}(y_3, x_3).$$
For brevity, we write $p(\mathbf{y})$ for $p(y_1, y_2, y_3)$. Thus, to
form the conditional distribution, within a normalization factor, we
simply include the observed variable values into the joint probability.
For vision applications, we often use such Markov chain structures to
describe events over time.

To capture relationships over space, a two-dimensional (2D) structure is
useful, called a **Markov random field** (MRF) @Blake2011:

![Two-dimensional Markov random field.](figures/graphical_models/mrf.png){width="48%" #fig-leafs}

Then the joint probability over all the variables factorizes into this
product: 

$$p(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{y}) = 
\frac{1}{p(\mathbf{y})}
\prod_{(i,j)} \phi_{ij}(x_i, x_j) \prod_i \psi_i(x_i, y_i),$$
where the first product is over all spatial neighbors $i$ and $j$, and the second
product is over all nodes $i$.

An example of how Markov random field models are applied to images is
depicted in @fig-leafs, which show a small image region and its context
in the image (@fig-leafs [a]). @fig-leafs [b] shows an MRF with each
node corresponding to a pixel of the image region. The states of an MRF
can be indicator variables of image segment membership for each pixel.
The states of a hypothetical most-probable configuration of this MRF are
shown as the color of each node in this illustration.

:::{#fig-leafs layout-ncol="2"}
![](figures/graphical_models/leaf2.jpg){width=97% #fig-leafs-a}

![](figures/graphical_models/leaf1.jpg){width=100% #fig-leafs-b}

Fig (a) Image to be segmented and a local region of (a) marked in red.  (b) Visualization of an MRF of nodes corresponding to image pixels inside the marked region, with states indicating segment membership, for a hypothetical most probable configuration.
::: 

## Directed Graphical Models

In addition to undirected graphical models, another type of graphical
model is commonly used. **Directed graphical models** @Koller2009
describe factorizations of the joint probability into products of
conditional probability distributions. Each node in a directed graph
contributes a well-specified factor in the joint probability: the
probability of its variable, conditioned on all the variables originating
arrows pointing into it. So this graph

![A directed graphical model with three variables.](figures/graphical_models/directed.png){width="20%" #eq-directedjoint}

denotes the joint probability,

elements: 3x3 grid of white spheres representing latent variables x_ij on the ground plane
3x3 grid of gray spheres representing observed variables y_ij elevated vertically above each x_ij
Vertical line segments connecting each latent node x_ij to its corresponding observed node y_ij
Horizontal and depth line segments connecting adjacent latent nodes x_ij to form the spatial grid
Fading/truncated wire segments extending outward from boundary nodes to indicate a larger/infinite grid
Text labels x1, x2, x3 floating near the back-row latent nodes
Text labels y1, y2, y3 floating near the back-row observed nodes
Color glows or halos around selected/highlighted nodes to represent probabilistic dependencies during interaction
Segment-color indicators (e.g., soft red/blue fills inside the spheres) to show node states under segmentation

interactions.teaches: Clicking a node highlights its Markov blanket (its immediate neighbors and observation), demonstrating that it is conditionally independent of all other nodes given this blanket.

interactions.label: Spatial Coupling
interactions.teaches: Controls how strongly adjacent nodes influence each other to share the same state; higher coupling smooths out noise into cohesive segments.

interactions.label: Observation Weight
interactions.teaches: Balances how much each latent node trusts its own local noisy observation versus its neighbors' consensus.

demo_steps.title: Two-Layer MRF Structure
demo_steps.narration: Observe the two-layer structure of the Markov Random Field. The bottom layer represents hidden/latent variables (the true pixel segments, x), while the top layer contains the noisy observations (the actual image pixels, y) connected by vertical pairwise potentials.

demo_steps.title: Markov Blanket & Independence
demo_steps.narration: Click on the center-back latent node x2. Notice how its Markov blanket lights up: its spatial neighbors (x1, x3, and the middle node) and its own observation (y2). Given these highlighted variables, x2 is completely shielded from—and conditionally independent of—the rest of the network.

demo_steps.title: Resolving Noisy Observations
demo_steps.narration: Let's introduce simulated noise (some nodes are colored red, others blue). When spatial coupling is low, the latent states faithfully match the noisy observations, resulting in a fragmented, speckled segmentation.

demo_steps.title: Cohesive Spatial Segmentation
demo_steps.narration: Now, increase the Spatial Coupling. As the neighbor-to-neighbor potential dominates, individual noisy outliers are overridden by the consensus of their neighbors, producing clean, contiguous spatial segments just like real image boundaries.

interactionPlan.view_reasoning: (1) The dominant layout in the source image is a 3x3 grid where horizontal grid lines run left-to-right, and the depth grid lines run diagonally down and left.
